about: Physics blocks whose maths is a formula (ND3b): each keeps its id, ports and results, and its maths is the Equation below, with a name that says what happens.

equation.name: Size of the boiling cells on a star's face

H.name: pressure scale height at the surface

explain.curious: The surface of a cool star is a boiling pan of bright cells. On the Sun each is about the size of France; on a red supergiant a few cells cover the whole star.
explain.science: Hot gas rises, spreads and sinks over about ten pressure scale heights: thin hot surfaces under strong gravity make small cells, cool distended ones make huge cells. The scale height is the same block an atmosphere uses, read at the photosphere.

params.description: the Sun's near-surface convective speed, m/s (a few km/s; Nordlund et al. 2009)
mean molecular weight of the photosphere (neutral solar mix about 1.3)

references: Nordlund, Å., Stein, R. F. and Asplund, M. 2009, Solar surface convection, Living Rev. Solar Phys. 6, 2: granules about 1 to 2 Mm across living minutes, with upflows of a few km/s near the surface. doi:10.12942/lrsp-2009-2

Freytag, B., Steffen, M. and Dorch, B. 2002, Spots on the surface of Betelgeuse: results from new 3D stellar convection models, Astron. Nachr. 323, 213: red supergiants have only a few giant convection cells across their faces. doi:10.1002/1521-3994(200208)323:3/4<213::AID-ASNA213>3.0.CO;2-H

equation.name: How fast the gas churns at a star's surface
equation.formula:
g_sun = GM_sun / (R_sun * R_sun)
w = v_sun * (T / T_sun) ^ (5/3) * cbrt(g_sun / g)
sound = sqrt(5/3 * k * T / (mu * m_u))
v = min(w, sound)

mu.name: mean molecular weight of the surface gas

source.text: Nordlund, Å., Stein, R. F. and Asplund, M. 2009, Solar surface convection, Living Rev. Solar Phys. 6, 2

explain.curious: The hotter the surface and the weaker its gravity, the faster it boils. On giant stars the gas churns nearly as fast as sound.
explain.science: The flux the surface must carry, σT⁴, is moved by rising gas as about ρv³. With photospheric density set by gravity over a fixed opacity, ρ ∝ gμ/T, so v ∝ T^(5/3) g^(−1/3), normalised to the Sun and capped at the sound speed.

params.description: life over the time to cross the cell (fixed so the Sun's granules live about 6 minutes)

references: Nordlund, Å., Stein, R. F. and Asplund, M. 2009, Solar surface convection, Living Rev. Solar Phys. 6, 2: granules about 1 to 2 Mm across living minutes, with upflows of a few km/s near the surface. doi:10.12942/lrsp-2009-2

equation.name: How long a boiling cell lasts

source.text: Nordlund, Å., Stein, R. F. and Asplund, M. 2009, Solar surface convection, Living Rev. Solar Phys. 6, 2

explain.curious: Each solar granule lives only minutes before it fades and a new one takes its place. Giant cells on a supergiant last months to years.
explain.science: A cell lasts about the time its gas takes to cross it.

params.description: supergranule over granule diameter (Sun: about 30 Mm over 1.2 Mm)

references: Rieutord, M. and Rincon, F. 2010, The Sun's supergranulation, Living Rev. Solar Phys. 7, 2: cells about 30 Mm across, lifetimes one to two days, horizontal flows about 300 to 400 m/s, outlined by the magnetic network. doi:10.12942/lrsp-2010-2
Gray, D. F. and Nagel, T. 1989, The granulation boundary in the H-R diagram, ApJ 341, 421: no granulation in stars hotter than about early F. doi:10.1086/167505

equation.name: Size of the big slow cells under the granules

source.text: Rieutord, M. and Rincon, F. 2010, The Sun's supergranulation, Living Rev. Solar Phys. 7, 2

explain.curious: Granules sit inside much bigger slow cells whose edges sweep the star's magnetic field into a glowing net. Spots and flares rise through that net.
explain.science: Supergranulation's origin is still debated; this block scales it with the granules, as the Sun shows, until better theory or observation of other stars replaces it.

params.description: supergranule flow over the granule speed (Sun: about 0.4 over 2 km/s)

equation.name: How long a big slow cell lasts

source.text: Rieutord, M. and Rincon, F. 2010, The Sun's supergranulation, Living Rev. Solar Phys. 7, 2

explain.curious: The Sun's big network cells last a day or two.
explain.science: The slow horizontal flow crosses a supergranule once in its life.
